chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Sa'id ibn 'Uqdah narrated to us, saying: Ali ibn al-Hasan at-Taymali narrated to me, saying: My two brothers Muhammad and Ahmad ibn al-Hasan narrated to me, from their father, from Tha'laba ibn Maymun, and from Jamee' ibn al-Kunasi all together, from Abu Baseer, from Kamil, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

Indeed, our Qa'im, when he rises, will invite the people to a new matter, just as the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) invited them to it. And indeed, Islam began as something strange, and it will return as something strange as it began. So, good news to the strangers.

key_terms.الْغُرَبَاءِ: The strangers (those who adhere to the truth when it is rare)
key_terms.قَائِمَنَا: Our Qa'im (the Rising One), referring to the Mahdi

ai.seo_question: What is the significance of Islam being described as 'strange' in Shia eschatology?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (AS) links the Mahdi’s call to a 'new matter' (amr jadid) with the cyclical nature of Islam’s visibility, echoing the Prophet’s hadith that Islam begins and returns as a stranger. This highlights the eschatological role of the Mahdi in restoring the pristine, uncorrupted practice of the faith, offering glad tidings to the faithful who remain distinct amidst societal deviation. The reference to 'new matter' suggests a renewal of divine authority and guidance, central to Shia expectations of the final Imam.
